claim: Figma (blog, 2019, self-reported design account, no figures): a central server is the authority, so arrival order decides and the last value sent wins per property; two clients changing the same property of one object conflict, unrelated properties do not.
Figma (blog, 2019, no rate given): simultaneous edits of one text value can lose a side, since from B, edits to AB and to BC end as AB or BC, never ABC.
Figma (blog, 2019, no figures): operational transforms were rejected as unnecessarily complex for its problem space, and the central server defines event order so no timestamp is needed.
Figma (blog, 2019, no figures): its multiplayer servers reject a parent update that would make a tree cycle, and each multiplayer document runs in its own server process.

Google Docs (Google Drive Blog posts, 2010, no figures): every edit is appended to a server revision log, and the server transforms a late change against changes committed since its editor's last sync and stores it as the next revision.

Google Docs (2010 posts, no figures): paragraph locks were rejected, because a lock sidesteps the technical challenges and two editors can both start believing they hold it, so one's changes must be merged or discarded.
Google Docs (2010 posts, no figures): a client sends at most one pending change at a time.

Google Docs (2010 posts, no figures): the posts state that if OT is implemented correctly, once all editors have received all changes, everyone sees the same document, a hedge the posts themselves make.
Potvin and Levenberg (Google, CACM 2016; self-reported): about one billion files, 35 million commits and 86TB, with about two billion lines of code in nine million source files, as of January 2015.

Potvin and Levenberg (Google, CACM 2016; self-reported): more than 25,000 developers commit 16,000 changes, automated systems commit another 24,000, and about 800,000 read queries per second at peak (the quoted line gives no period for the commit counts).

Potvin and Levenberg (Google, CACM 2016): all changes enter one trunk in a single serial order, visible to every developer right after commit, and long-lived parallel branches are exceedingly rare (no rate given).

Potvin and Levenberg (Google, CACM 2016): on almost every change an automated system rebuilds all affected dependencies, and a change causing widespread build breakage is automatically undone (no before-and-after figure given).

Jaspan and others (Google, ICSE-SEIP 2018, survey and logs; self-reported): engineers commit to the head of a trunk-based repository, and projects use whatever version of a dependency is at the repo head.

Microsoft (Brian Harry, DevBlogs 2017; self-reported): about 3.5M files, a 300GB repo and about 4,000 engineers; vanilla Git commands took 30 minutes up to hours and a few never completed, and the post says most are now less than 20 seconds.

Microsoft (Brian Harry, DevBlogs 2017; self-reported): Windows cross-branch merges reached 10,000's of changes with 1,000's of conflicts, and the pull-request and conflict UI did not scale to them in the first week.
Discord (blog, 2017; self-reported): per-column last-write-wins with upserts let an edit and a delete at the same moment leave a message row with only its primary key and text.

Discord (blog, 2023; self-reported): the stated pressure was hot read partitions, since in Cassandra reads cost more than writes and concurrent reads can hotspot a partition; the post names no write contention.

Discord (blog, 2023; self-reported; database and service layer changed together, no workload given): 177 Cassandra nodes became 72 ScyllaDB nodes, history fetch p99 went from 40-125ms to 15ms, and migration ran at up to 3.2 million per second, nine days against an estimated three months for the stock tool.

Discord (blog, 2023, no figure given): data services coalesce identical concurrent requests into one query and route by consistent hashing on channel id, so one instance sees every request for a channel.

Meta server-side rebase on push: only a third party's notes of a 2015 Facebook talk say Facebook moved to rebasing on the server at push to remove the pull, rebase and retry race; no Meta primary text was found and no figure is given.
Facebook (Mercurial post, 2014; self-reported): the status command ran more than 5x faster than Git's, and clone and pull 10x faster; these are file-scan and clone figures, not landing figures.
